title: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
summary: Why C pointer bugs and data races compile and ship, how Rust's types catch them, what unsafe unlocks, how to build sound abstractions such as a Vec, and how to wrap real C libraries.
outcomes: Explain why use after free and out-of-bounds bugs compile cleanly in C and how Rust reports the same code
Map C pointer roles to Box, &T, &mut T, slices and raw pointers, and replace goto cleanup with Drop and ?
Explain how the borrow rules plus Send and Sync rule out data races, and which race conditions remain
List the five operations unsafe unlocks and explain why breaking aliasing rules miscompiles
Judge whether an unsafe-backed function is sound, using split_at_mut and module privacy as models
Build a minimal Vec on raw allocation with documented invariants and check it under Miri
Write an FFI call that keeps ownership and layout correct with CString and #[repr(C)]
Wrap a C library with build.rs, cc, bindgen, an owning handle and panic-safe callbacks

lessons.title: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship

blocks.md:
You already know the Rust side: one owner per value, drop at end of scope, many readers or one writer. This course puts that next to C, the language most systems code is still written in, and then opens the escape hatch Rust keeps for the cases its checker cannot prove: `unsafe`.

In C a pointer is just an address. The type `char *` says nothing about whether the holder must call `free`, whether the block is still alive, or how many bytes it covers. The compiler checks none of that.

A quick recall of the C you need. `malloc(n)` returns a pointer to `n` uninitialized bytes on the heap, or NULL if it fails, and `free(p)` gives the block back. `free` takes only the pointer, no size: the allocator keeps that bookkeeping itself, so the pointer is the only handle. A C string is a run of bytes ending in a zero byte (`'\0'`), the terminator: `strcpy` copies up to and including it, `strlen` counts the bytes before it, and `printf("%s")` prints until it. None of these functions know how big the buffer behind the pointer is.

blocks.caption: Compiles with no warnings under clang -Wall -Wextra, the flags that switch on most of its warnings. Line 12 reads freed memory.

blocks.title: Use after free: a stale pointer reads someone else's data

scenes.caption: `malloc(8)` returns block A and `name` holds its address. Nothing in the program records that `name` is responsible for freeing it. Simplified: allocator metadata is not shown.
`strcpy` writes the 5 letters of alice plus the terminating zero byte into block A.
`alias = name` copies the address. Both pointers look identical to the compiler; neither is marked as the owner.
`free(name)` hands block A back to the allocator. Nothing erases it (simplified: the allocator may write bookkeeping into it) and both variables still hold address A, but both are now dangling.
The next `malloc(8)` of the same size got block A back in our -O0 (optimizer off) run on macOS. Reuse is up to the allocator, which is why the bug is intermittent.
`strcpy(other, "mallory")` overwrites the block with 7 letters and a zero byte. The new owner did nothing wrong.

`printf("%s", alias)` reads through the stale pointer and prints mallory: data that belongs to another part of the program. In an attacker's hands this is a read or write primitive: a dependable way to read or overwrite memory of their choosing.

blocks.md: Keep three build modes in mind before you guess. Besides the `-O0` build above, `-O2` is the usual optimized level. **AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address`) makes the compiler insert a check before every memory access against *shadow memory*, a side table that records which heap bytes are currently allocated. Touching a freed block then stops the program with a report instead of reading whatever is there.

blocks.prompt: What does this program print? Think about it before revealing: the C standard calls line 12 undefined behavior.
blocks.reveal:
It depends, which is exactly the problem. On our macOS test machine an unoptimized build (-O0) printed **mallory**, the next owner's data. The same source built with -O2 printed **a single garbage byte** (0x02 on that run, so the line looked empty). Built with AddressSanitizer, it stopped with `heap-use-after-free` at line 12 and also reported where the block was freed (line 9) and allocated (line 6).

**Undefined behavior** (UB) means the language standard places no requirement on what happens, so the optimizer may assume it never occurs. The program is not "slightly wrong"; it has no meaning.

blocks.md:
The same root cause, a pointer whose validity nobody tracks, produces a family of bugs:

- **Use after free**: reading or writing a block after `free`.
- **Double free**: calling `free` twice, which corrupts allocator state.
- **Out of bounds**: indexing past the end, because a pointer does not carry a length.
- **Uninitialized read**: using bytes nothing wrote.
- **Data race**: two threads touching the same memory, at least one writing, with no synchronization.

blocks.title: Share of security bugs that are memory safety bugs

scenes.caption: Chromium: around 70% of high and critical severity security bugs (912 bugs since 2015) are memory unsafety, and half of those are use after free, so roughly 35%.
Android: memory safety bugs were 76% of its vulnerabilities in 2019, in line with the roughly 70% industry norm the Android team cites.
After new Android code moved mostly to memory safe languages (Rust, Java, Kotlin), the share fell to 24% in 2024, even though most existing code is still C and C++.

blocks.md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.
C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

blocks.question: A C function returns `char *`. What does its type tell the caller about freeing the result?
options: The caller must free it, because it is a non-const pointer
Nothing: ownership is only in the documentation, the compiler cannot check it
The function frees it when the caller returns
It must be freed with the allocator that matches its type
blocks.explain: A raw C pointer carries no ownership or lifetime information. Whether the caller must call `free`, must not, or must call a library specific function is a convention written in docs. That gap is what makes leaks, double frees and use after free easy to write.

blocks.question: The Android team kept most of its existing C and C++ code but wrote new code in memory safe languages. What happened to the memory safety share of its vulnerabilities between 2019 and 2024?
options: It stayed near 70%, because old code still dominates
It rose, because FFI glue introduced new bugs
It fell from 76% to 24%
It fell to 0%, because Rust code has no unsafe
blocks.explain: The September 2024 Google Security Blog post reports 76% in 2019 and 24% in 2024. Their explanation: most vulnerabilities live in new or recently changed code, and vulnerability density decays as code ages, so stopping the inflow of new unsafe code pays off quickly.

lessons.title: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through

blocks.md: Rust splits C's single pointer type `T *` into several pointer types, each carrying the information C leaves in comments. Recall from the prerequisite: a borrow (`&T` or `&mut T`) may not outlive its owner, and you can have many `&T` or one `&mut T`, never both.

blocks.title: One C pointer type, five Rust pointer types

scenes.caption: In C all five of these are spelled `T *` (plus maybe `const`). The meaning lives in comments and conventions.
An owning heap pointer becomes `Box<T>`: exactly one owner, and the drop at end of scope is the only `free`. Double free cannot be written in safe code.
Read-only and read-write arguments become `&T` and `&mut T`. The borrow checker proves they never outlive the owner and that a `&mut` is never aliased.
Pointer plus separate length becomes a slice, a fat pointer that stores both. Every `s[i]` is bounds checked against that length.
Anything the compiler cannot reason about stays a raw pointer, which behaves like C's. Creating one is safe; dereferencing one requires `unsafe` (lesson 4).

blocks.md: Here is lesson 1's use after free, translated. `drop(name)` is Rust's explicit way to end ownership early; it is a move, so the compiler checks it against outstanding borrows.

blocks.caption: Real rustc output, abbreviated. The bug is reported at compile time with all three lines that form it.

blocks.md: Ownership also removes C's most tedious chore: releasing everything on every exit path. A C function that opens a file, allocates a buffer and takes a lock (a **mutex**: only one thread can hold it at a time, and the others wait in their lock call until it is released) must undo exactly the steps that succeeded, in reverse, on each early return. The usual idiom is a chain of `goto` labels at the bottom of the function, one per resource.

blocks.caption: Compiles with no warnings under clang -Wall -Wextra and returns 0 for a readable file, -1 for a missing one. Each failure jumps to the label that undoes only what was acquired.

blocks.prompt: A teammate rejects short files by adding `if (n < 16) return -1;` right after the `fread` line. It compiles cleanly. What does that new return leave behind?
blocks.reveal: Three things. The 4096-byte `buf` leaks, the `FILE` stays open (a file descriptor leak), and the mutex stays **locked forever**, so the next caller of `load` blocks for good. The compiler cannot object: in C, a `return` and a resource are unrelated as far as the type system knows. The correct edit is `goto unlock;`, and every reviewer has to check that by hand.

blocks.caption: Ran and printed true three times. The `?` operator returns the error early, and the Rust Reference guarantees that leaving a scope drops its variables in reverse order of declaration, so the guard unlocks, the Vec frees and the File closes on every path.

blocks.md: Not every bug can be ruled out before the program runs. An index computed from input is the classic case. Rust's answer is a **run-time check** that turns undefined behavior into a defined failure: a **panic**, which unwinds the thread (or aborts) with a message. **Unwinding** walks back up the call stack and runs each frame's drop code, so memory is still freed and locks released; **abort** ends the process at once instead.

blocks.title: An index the compiler cannot know: Rust checks it at run time

scenes.caption: `v` is a `Vec<i32>`: pointer, length 3, capacity 3. The length travels with the pointer.
The index comes from run-time input (argument count 1, plus 4), so no compile-time check can catch it.
`v[i]` compares 5 against the stored length 3 before touching memory and panics. The process exits with status 101 instead of reading past the buffer.
scenes.output:
thread 'main' panicked at oob.rs:4:21:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 5

blocks.prompt: The C version (`int v[3]`, `printf("%d", v[argc + 4])`) compiled with one unrelated warning. What did it print?
blocks.reveal: An arbitrary integer: whatever 4 bytes happened to sit 8 bytes past the end of the array (on our run, 911781002), and it exited with status 0 as if nothing went wrong. Silent wrong answers are worse than crashes, because nothing tells you to look.

blocks.title: Pointer sizes on a 64-bit target (bytes, rustc measured)

scenes.caption: A reference, a Box and a raw pointer are each one 8-byte address. A slice reference is 16 bytes: address plus length. That length is what makes bounds checks possible.
`Option<Box<u8>>` is still 8 bytes: Box is never null, so None is stored as the null address. `Option<*const u8>` needs 16 bytes, because a raw pointer may already be null.

blocks.md:
Safe Rust's promise is narrower than "no bugs". It rules out undefined behavior: no use after free, no double free, no out-of-bounds access, no data races (lesson 3 shows how). These remain possible and are considered memory safe:

- **Leaks**: `Rc` cycles or `Box::leak` keep memory alive forever. The Rust Book states that preventing leaks is not one of Rust's guarantees.
- **Panics**: a failed bounds check is a crash, just a defined one.
- **Integer overflow**: debug builds panic; release builds wrap in two's complement (255u8 + 1 becomes 0) unless you use `checked_*` or `wrapping_*` methods.
- **Logic bugs and deadlocks**.

Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

blocks.question: Which bug does safe Rust still allow, by design?
options: Reading an element past the end of a `Vec`
Two threads writing the same `i32` without a lock
A leak from two `Rc` values that point at each other
Using a `String` after it has been dropped
blocks.explain: Out-of-bounds access becomes a panic, sharing mutable data across threads without a lock or atomic fails to compile, and use after drop is a borrow error. Leaks are explicitly memory safe in Rust: an `Rc` cycle never reaches count 0, so its memory is never freed.

blocks.question: Why can `Option<&T>` be passed to C as a plain nullable pointer, but `Option<*const T>` cannot?
options: A reference is never null, so None can use the null address and the Option stays one pointer wide
References are always 16 bytes
C cannot read Rust enums of any kind
Raw pointers are not allowed inside Option
blocks.explain: The std `Option` docs guarantee that `Option<&T>`, `Option<&mut T>`, `Option<Box<T>>` and `Option<NonNull<T>>` (`NonNull<T>` is a raw pointer guaranteed not to be null) have the same size, alignment and ABI (application binary interface) as the inner pointer, with None as null; the ABI is how a value is laid out and passed between compiled functions. A raw pointer can already be null, so Option needs a separate tag (we measured 16 bytes).

lessons.title: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 listed data races among C's bug classes, and lesson 2 claimed safe Rust rules them out. Here is the mechanism. The tiny example: two threads each add 1 to a shared counter a million times. The answer should be 2,000,000.

In C the threads come from **pthreads** (POSIX threads, the standard thread API on Unix-like systems): `pthread_create` starts a thread running a function and `pthread_join` waits for it to finish.

blocks.caption: No warnings under clang -Wall -Wextra. Five runs of the -O0 build printed 1070465, 1013129, 997754, 1005246 and 1032789: roughly half the increments lost, a different amount each time.

blocks.md: The C standard (C11 and later) defines the bug precisely. Two accesses to the same memory location **conflict** if at least one is a write. A program with two conflicting accesses has a **data race** unless both are atomic operations or one *happens before* the other (for example because a mutex unlock in one thread precedes the lock in the other). If a data race occurs, the behavior is undefined.

blocks.title: counter++ from two threads: a lost update, then a lock

scenes.caption: `counter++` is three machine steps: load the value, add 1 in a register, store it back. Thread 1 loads 7. Simplified: one round of the loop, with an example value.
Before thread 1 stores, thread 2 loads the same 7. Nothing in the C program orders these two loads.
Thread 1 adds 1 and stores 8.
Thread 2 also computed 7 + 1 and stores 8. Two increments ran, the counter grew by one: a lost update. Repeat that across a million iterations and the total falls far short.
With a mutex around the increment, only one thread can be between lock and unlock. Thread 1 does its whole load, add, store as one unit.
Thread 2's lock call waits until thread 1 unlocks, then it sees 9 and stores 10. No update is lost, and unlock-then-lock orders the two accesses, so this is not a data race.

blocks.prompt: The same file built with `-O2` printed 2000000 on three runs in a row. Is the race fixed?
blocks.reveal:
No. Reading the generated assembly shows why the answer looked right: the optimizer, allowed to assume no data race exists, replaced the whole loop with one load, one add of 1,000,000 and one store. The window between load and store is now a few instructions instead of a million, so the threads rarely collide, but when they do, a full million increments vanish at once.

Built with ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread -g -O1`), the program printed `WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race`, pointing at line 9 (`counter++`) in both threads.

blocks.md: **ThreadSanitizer** (TSan) is clang's race detector: the compiler instruments every memory access and a run-time library tracks which thread touched which address under which locks. Clang's docs put its typical cost at a 5x to 15x slowdown and 5x to 10x memory. Like AddressSanitizer, it only sees the interleavings that actually run. Now the same program in Rust.

blocks.caption: Real rustc errors, abbreviated. The spawned thread may outlive main's stack frame, and main and the thread would both hold write access to counter.

blocks.md: Two separate checks fire. `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `'static` (it may hold no borrows of local variables), because the new thread can outlive the function that started it. Even with `thread::scope`, whose threads are guaranteed to finish before the scope ends and so may borrow locals, two closures that both capture `&mut counter` fail with E0499, the prerequisite's one-writer rule. A data race needs two threads that reach the same memory with at least one writing. That is aliasing plus mutation, which the borrow rules already forbid; the Rustonomicon (the official guide to writing unsafe Rust, published alongside the Rust Book) says data races are prevented mostly by ownership alone.

blocks.prompt: Add `move` to the first closure: `thread::spawn(move || ...)`. It compiles. What does it print?
blocks.reveal: **1000000**. `u64` is `Copy`, so `move` copied the counter into the closure. The thread incremented its own private copy, which was thrown away; main's loop did the other million. rustc warned `unused variable: counter` with the hint *did you mean to capture by reference instead?*. No memory was shared, so there was no race, only a logic bug.

blocks.md:
Interior mutability (`Cell`, `RefCell`, `Rc`'s counter) allows mutation through a shared reference, so the borrow rules alone are not enough. Two **marker traits** (traits with no methods that only label a type) fill the gap:

- **Send**: a value of this type can be moved to another thread safely.
- **Sync**: the type can be shared between threads by reference; precisely, `T` is Sync if and only if `&T` is Send.

Both are **auto traits**: a type made entirely of Send fields is Send automatically, and the same for Sync. The exceptions the Rustonomicon lists: raw pointers are neither, `Rc` is neither, and `UnsafeCell` (the primitive that `Cell` and `RefCell` are built on, lesson 4) is not Sync, so neither are they. `thread::spawn` demands `F: Send + 'static`, so everything the closure captures must be Send.

blocks.caption: Real rustc output, abbreviated. Two Rc clones on two threads would update one reference count without atomics; the trait bound stops it at compile time.

blocks.title: Which shared-ownership types may cross threads

scenes.caption: Single-threaded tools from the prerequisite: Rc shares ownership, RefCell checks borrows at run time. Both update a counter with ordinary, non-atomic writes.
Two threads holding clones of one Rc would both update its reference count at once: a data race. So Rc is neither Send nor Sync, and Arc, whose count uses atomic operations, takes its place.
RefCell may be moved to one thread (it is Send when T is), but a shared &RefCell would let two threads bump its borrow flag at once, so it is not Sync. Mutex is Sync: each access takes a lock.
Arc only makes the ownership thread-safe, not the contents: Arc<T> is Send only if T is Send and Sync. Arc<RefCell<T>> is rejected; Arc<Mutex<T>> is the standard shared counter.

blocks.caption: Prints 2000000 every run. A lighter fix for a plain counter is `AtomicU64::fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)`, one indivisible read-modify-write (Relaxed: atomic, but no ordering of other memory), which also printed 2000000.

blocks.md: Swap the Mutex for a RefCell and rustc refuses: `` `RefCell<u64>` cannot be shared between threads safely ``, with the note *if you want to do aliasing and mutation between multiple threads, use std::sync::RwLock instead*. The `Arc` docs explain the design: Arc makes it thread-safe to have several owners of the same data, but it does not add thread safety to the data itself.

Implementing Send or Sync by hand is `unsafe impl Send for MyType {}`, one of the five powers in lesson 4. The compiler cannot check it, and the Rustonomicon warns that an incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior: you are promising that every way to reach the type from two threads is synchronized.

What safe Rust still allows is a **race condition**: a result that depends on thread timing. Deadlocks (two threads each waiting for a lock the other holds) and check-then-act bugs (read a shared index, check it, read it again after another thread changed it) compile fine. The Rustonomicon calls preventing them in general impossible when you do not control the scheduler. They stay memory safe unless unsafe code trusts the stale check, for example by skipping a bounds check with `get_unchecked`.

Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

blocks.question: Which of these compiles and shares one counter between two spawned threads?
options: Clones of an `Arc<RefCell<u64>>` moved into each thread
Clones of an `Rc<Mutex<u64>>` moved into each thread
Two `thread::scope` threads that each capture `&mut counter`
Clones of an `Arc<Mutex<u64>>` moved into each thread
blocks.explain: Arc<RefCell> fails because RefCell is not Sync, so Arc of it is not Send. Rc<Mutex> fails because Rc is not Send. Two scoped closures that both mutably borrow the counter fail with E0499. Arc gives thread-safe shared ownership and Mutex serializes each access.

blocks.question: Why is `RefCell<T>` Send (when T is Send) but not Sync?
options: RefCell allocates on the heap, which threads cannot share
Its borrow flag is updated without atomics: moving it leaves one thread in charge, but sharing `&RefCell` lets two threads update the flag at once
Sync requires a type to have no methods that take `&mut self`
RefCell panics on conflicting borrows, and panics cannot cross threads
blocks.explain: Moving a RefCell to another thread leaves exactly one thread able to touch it, so Send is fine. Sync means `&RefCell<T>` could be used from two threads at once, and its run-time borrow bookkeeping is ordinary non-atomic memory: that would be a data race.

lessons.title: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker

blocks.md: Static analysis is conservative: the compiler would rather reject a correct program than accept a wrong one. And the hardware itself (device registers, system calls, C libraries) knows nothing about ownership. So Rust contains a second language, **unsafe Rust**, entered with the `unsafe` keyword.

The Rust Book lists exactly five things an `unsafe` block or function allows that safe Rust does not:

1. Dereference a raw pointer (`*const T`, `*mut T`).
2. Call an `unsafe` function or method.
3. Access or modify a mutable `static` variable.
4. Implement an `unsafe` trait (such as `Send` or `Sync` from lesson 3: a wrong `unsafe impl Send` lets safe code race on data the type does not protect).
5. Access fields of a `union`.

Misconception: "`unsafe` turns off the borrow checker." It does not. References inside an unsafe block are checked exactly as before: two `&mut x` in an `unsafe` block still fail with E0499 (cannot borrow as mutable more than once), and rustc also warns that the block is unnecessary. `unsafe` only unlocks the five operations above.

Raw pointers are the C pointers of Rust. Unlike references, they may alias freely (several `*mut T` to one place), may be null, may dangle, and never free anything on their own. The `&raw const x` and `&raw mut x` operators create them directly.

blocks.caption: Prints 7. Without the unsafe block, `*a += 1` is error E0133: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe function or block.

blocks.title: Raw pointers: two writers to one place, and a wild address

scenes.caption: `let mut x = 5`. Two `&mut x` at once would be rejected with E0499, even inside an unsafe block.
`&raw mut x` twice gives two `*mut i32` aimed at x. Raw pointers ignore the borrowing rules, and creating them needs no unsafe.
`*a += 1` inside `unsafe`: you, not the compiler, vouch that a points to a live, aligned i32 (aligned: at an address that is a multiple of 4, the size of an i32) and that no reference to x is in use.
`*b += 1` writes through the second pointer. Single-threaded and with no live references, this is fine; the program prints 7.
Casting the integer 0x12345 to `*const i32` is also safe. Dereferencing it is undefined behavior: there may be nothing mapped there, or the optimizer may delete the access.

blocks.md: An **unsafe function** is one with a precondition the compiler cannot check, written as `unsafe fn`. Calling it requires an `unsafe` block, which is your signature that you read the contract and meet it. Standard example: `Vec::set_len(n)` is unsafe because it requires `n <= capacity()` and that the elements up to `n` are initialized; break either and later reads touch garbage. Since the 2024 edition the body of an `unsafe fn` is not itself an unsafe context (the `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` lint warns), so the code inside still wraps each unsafe operation in its own `unsafe` block, as below.

blocks.caption: Idiom from the Rust Book: an unsafe fn documents its contract, and every unsafe block says in a SAFETY comment why the contract holds.

blocks.md:
What exactly must you avoid? The Rust Reference keeps a list of **behavior considered undefined**, which applies to unsafe code too. Highlights:

- Data races.
- Accessing memory through a dangling or misaligned pointer.
- Breaking the aliasing rules: memory behind a live `&T` must not be mutated (outside `UnsafeCell`, the one std type that permits mutation through a shared reference; `Cell`, `RefCell` and `Mutex` are built on it), and a live `&mut T` must be the only way to reach its memory.
- Producing an invalid value, for example a `bool` that is not 0 or 1, or a null reference.

The Reference warns the list is not exhaustive.

Why are the aliasing rules worth that much care? Because the optimizer relies on them. The Rustonomicon's example: in `compute(input: &u32, output: &mut u32)`, a `&mut` that is the only path to its memory means writing `*output` cannot change `*input`, so the compiler may read `*input` once and keep it in a register. Below, unsafe code breaks the rule by making both references point at the same `x`.

blocks.caption: Compiles; the only unsafe operations are turning the raw pointer into two references. We ran a debug build and an optimized (-O) build with rustc 1.90. Predict before reading on.

blocks.prompt: Read `compute` in source order with `input` and `output` both pointing at `x = 20`. Which build matches the source, and why does the other differ?
blocks.reveal:
Source order gives **1**: `20 > 10` sets x to 1, then the second test reads the new value, `1 > 5` is false. The debug build printed 1.

The optimized build printed **2**. Same source, two answers. Trusting that `output` cannot alias `input`, the compiler kept the first read of `*input` (20), so both tests passed and 1 was doubled. Neither answer is "right"; the program broke a rule the optimizer is allowed to assume.

blocks.md: Miri, the undefined-behavior detector covered in the next lesson, rejects this program at the call: `Undefined Behavior: trying to retag from <552> for SharedReadOnly permission at alloc205[0x0], but that tag does not exist in the borrow stack for this location`. The *borrow stack* comes from **Stacked Borrows**, the experimental model of Rust's aliasing rules that Miri checks by default; **Tree Borrows** is an alternative model (`-Zmiri-tree-borrows`) that also flags it, as a forbidden write access.

`unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

blocks.question: Which line needs an `unsafe` block?
options: `let p = 0x1000usize as *const u8;`
`let n = v.len();` on a `Vec<u8>`
`v.set_len(4);` on a `Vec<u8>`
`let r = &raw const x;`
blocks.explain: Creating raw pointers (by cast or with `&raw`) is safe: nothing happens until you dereference. `set_len` is an `unsafe fn` because it trusts you that the new length is within capacity and the elements are initialized, so calling it needs an unsafe block.

blocks.question: A teammate wraps a function body in `unsafe { ... }` to silence E0502 (a shared and a mutable borrow overlap). What happens?
options: It compiles, because unsafe disables borrow checking in the block
It still fails with E0502; unsafe does not relax the borrow rules on references
It compiles but inserts a run-time borrow check
It compiles only in release mode
blocks.explain: The Book is explicit: unsafe does not turn off the borrow checker or other safety checks on references. To express aliasing the checker cannot verify, you must switch to raw pointers (or `UnsafeCell` based types) and take responsibility for the rules yourself.

lessons.title: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness

blocks.md: Most unsafe code exists to build a **safe abstraction**: a function or type with a safe API whose implementation uses a few unsafe operations the checker cannot verify. `Vec`, `String`, `split_at_mut` and the standard library's locks all work this way.

The Rust Book's example: split one mutable slice into two mutable halves. The obvious safe version, `(&mut values[..mid], &mut values[mid..])`, is rejected with E0499 (cannot borrow `*values` as mutable more than once). The checker sees two `&mut` borrows of the same slice; it does not reason that the index ranges are disjoint.

blocks.caption: Rust Book Listing 20-6. The function is not marked unsafe, so any safe code may call it.

blocks.title: split_at_mut: two disjoint mutable halves from one pointer

scenes.caption: `v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, len 6. Cells 6 to 9 are memory past the buffer that v does not own.
`as_mut_ptr()` yields a `*mut i32` to element 0. `assert!(mid <= len)` checks 3 <= 6 before any unsafe code runs.
`from_raw_parts_mut(ptr, 3)` builds the left slice over indices 0 to 2.
`ptr.add(3)` and length 6 - 3 = 3 build the right slice over indices 3 to 5. The two ranges do not overlap, so two `&mut` are sound.
Callers use them like any slices: `left[0] = 10; right[0] = 40;` leaves v as [10, 2, 3, 40, 5, 6]. The caller never wrote unsafe.

Delete the assert and call with mid = 8 in a release build: left claims 8 elements (2 past the end); right starts at index 8 with length 6 - 8, which a 64-bit usize wraps to 2^64 - 2 = 18446744073709551614. Both slices are invalid: undefined behavior.

blocks.prompt: Remove `assert!(mid <= len)` and call `split_at_mut(&mut v, 8)` on the 6-element vector. What happens in a debug build versus a release build?
blocks.reveal:
**Debug:** the subtraction `len - mid` is `6 - 8` on `usize`, which panics with *attempt to subtract with overflow*. Luck, not design: the overflow check fired before the bad slice was used.

**Release (-O):** overflow checks are off, so `6 - 8` wraps to 18446744073709551614. Our run printed `8 18446744073709551614` as the two lengths. Both slices point at memory v does not own. That is undefined behavior reachable from safe code, which makes the function **unsound**.

blocks.md: The Rust Reference defines the bar: unsafe code is **sound** if no safe code that calls it can trigger undefined behavior; otherwise it is **unsound**. The `assert!` is not decoration. It is the proof that every pointer built inside the unsafe block stays in bounds.

blocks.title: One safe-code edit makes the unsafe block unsound

scenes.caption: Example from the Rustonomicon, the official guide to unsafe Rust. With the original `<`, index(4) fails the test 4 < 4 and returns None, so the unchecked read only runs for idx 0 to 3: sound.
Someone edits only the safe comparison to `<=`. Now 4 <= 4 is true and control enters the unsafe block.

`get_unchecked(4)` reads one byte past the array: undefined behavior. A debug build caught it with a standard library precondition check; an optimized build on our machine died on a trap instruction, one planted to crash the program on purpose.
scenes.output:
thread 'main' panicked at idx.rs:3:28:
unsafe precondition(s) violated: slice::get_unchecked requires that the index is within the slice

blocks.md:
The lesson from that example is that safety is **non-local**: the unsafe block's correctness depends on state set up by ordinary safe code around it. The Rustonomicon makes the same point with a hand-written `Vec { ptr, len, cap }`: `push` writes at `ptr.add(len)` assuming `cap` matches the allocation. A 100% safe private method that does `self.cap += 1` breaks that assumption. Lesson 6 builds that Vec end to end.

The fix is **privacy**. If `cap` is a private field, only code in the same module can touch it, so the audit boundary is the module, not the whole program.

Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

**Miri** is the official tool for finding undefined behavior in unsafe code. The name is short for MIR interpreter: MIR is the mid-level intermediate representation rustc lowers your code to, and Miri executes it step by step while tracking every allocation and pointer. It interprets your program or test suite and flags violations such as dangling pointers, out-of-bounds access and aliasing rule breaks. It needs the nightly toolchain, the daily development build of the compiler that ships experimental components like Miri; `rustup`, Rust's toolchain installer, adds it (`rustup +nightly component add miri`, then `cargo +nightly miri test`).

A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

blocks.question: Which change can make a sound module containing a hand-written `Vec` unsound, without touching any unsafe block?
options: Adding a private method that returns `self.len`
Adding a `pub fn set_cap(&mut self, c: usize)` that assigns `self.cap = c`
Renaming the `push` method
Adding a test that pushes 1000 elements
blocks.explain: The unsafe code in `push` trusts `cap` to match the real allocation. A public setter lets any safe caller break that invariant and make `push` write out of bounds. Reading `len` cannot break anything, and tests do not change the code's soundness.

blocks.question: Your unsafe-backed parser passes `cargo miri test` with no errors. What can you conclude?
options: The parser can never cause undefined behavior
The inputs your tests ran did not trigger any UB that Miri detects
The parser is safe to mark `Sync`
The borrow checker has verified the unsafe blocks
blocks.explain: Miri checks the executions it actually performs. Untested inputs, and kinds of unsoundness Miri does not model, can still hide bugs. It raises confidence; it does not prove soundness.

lessons.title: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch

blocks.md: Lesson 5 judged soundness from two short functions. Now build a whole unsafe-backed type, following the Rustonomicon's Vec chapter. The tiny example: push the words a, b, c, d, e and watch three numbers. A Vec is a **pointer** to a heap block, a **capacity** (how many slots the block has room for) and a **length** (how many slots hold a value). Slots between len and cap are allocated but empty.

blocks.title: MyVec<String>: slots, cap and len as you push five words

scenes.caption: `MyVec::new()` allocates nothing. `ptr` holds `NonNull::dangling()`, a non-null placeholder address, and cap 0 marks that there is no allocation.
push(a): len == cap, so grow. cap 0 becomes 1 with `alloc` (A, A2, A4, A8 stand for block addresses), then `write` puts a into slot 0 and len becomes 1.
push(b): full again. `realloc` grows the block to 2 slots (it may move it, so ptr changes), keeping a; b goes into slot 1.
push(c): cap doubles to 4. Slot 3 is allocated but **uninitialized**: no String lives there yet, only whatever bytes the allocator left.
push(d): room exists, no grow. `write` fills slot 3 and len reaches cap.
push(e): cap doubles to 8. Invariant: the first len slots hold valid Strings; slots len to cap - 1 hold nothing.
pop(): len drops to 4 first, then `ptr::read` copies e out to the caller. Slot 4 still holds e's bytes, but it is now logically uninitialized.
Drop: pop the 4 live Strings (each one frees its own text), then `dealloc` the 8-slot block with the same Layout that allocated it.
Block returned to the allocator. Every String was dropped exactly once and nothing was read from an uninitialized slot.

blocks.md:
Three std pieces do the low-level work, each introduced where the code needs it:

- [`NonNull<T>`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/struct.NonNull.html): in the docs' words, `*mut T` but non-zero and covariant. Non-zero lets `Option<MyVec<T>>` use null for None; *covariant* means a `MyVec<&'static str>` can be used where a `MyVec<&'a str>` is expected, as with std's Vec. With no allocation yet, `NonNull::dangling()` supplies an aligned, non-null placeholder.
- **`Layout`**: the size and alignment of an allocation request. `Layout::array::<T>(n)` computes it for n elements and refuses sizes past `isize::MAX` bytes.
- **`alloc`, `realloc`, `dealloc`** in `std::alloc`: the global allocator. Asking it for zero bytes is undefined behavior, which is why cap 0 means "no allocation" instead of a zero-sized block.

blocks.caption: First half of the type (it compiles and runs with the second half). Every unsafe block names the invariant it relies on. Grows 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 as in the figure.

blocks.md: Writing into a slot is the subtle part. `*slot = value` is an assignment, and assignment first **drops the old value** at that place. A fresh slot has no old value, only leftover bytes, so for a String that would mean freeing whatever garbage address those bytes form. [`ptr::write`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/fn.write.html) overwrites the memory without reading or dropping what was there. In the other direction, `ptr::read` copies the bits out as a value; `pop` shrinks `len` first, so the slot it read from counts as empty.

blocks.caption: Second half. Drop pops every live element (running each String's own drop) before giving the block back with the same Layout.

blocks.prompt: Replace `.write(value)` in `push` with the assignment `*self.ptr.as_ptr().add(self.len) = value;`. It still compiles, and the unit test (push five Strings, pop one, drop) **passes** under `cargo test`. What does `cargo +nightly miri test` say?
blocks.reveal:
It stops inside `push`: `Undefined Behavior: reading memory at alloc40502[0x8..0x10], but memory is uninitialized`. The backtrace runs from `push` into `drop_glue::<String>` (the compiler-generated code that drops a value): the assignment tried to drop a String that was never there, reading its pointer field from uninitialized memory.

The normal test passed by luck: whatever the allocator left in those bytes did not crash this run.

blocks.md: That is the routine for unsafe-backed code: unit tests that exercise growth, pop and drop, run under Miri (`cargo +nightly miri test`). Besides UB, Miri reports memory that is still allocated when the program ends. Two more planted bugs show both kinds of report.

blocks.title: Three planted bugs, three Miri reports

scenes.caption: The test pushes a, b, c, d, e as Strings, pops e, and drops the vector. The correct code passes both `cargo test` and `cargo +nightly miri test`.
scenes.output:
test tests::push_pop_strings ... ok
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed

scenes.caption: Bug 1: line 3 becomes `*slot = value`. Assignment first drops the old String in the slot, but there is none: the drop reads uninitialized bytes as a pointer. Plain `cargo test` still passed.
scenes.output: error: Undefined Behavior: reading memory at alloc40502[0x8..0x10], but memory is uninitialized at [0x8..0x10], and this operation requires initialized memory

scenes.caption: Bug 2: line 2 grows only when len == 0. The second push writes slot 1 of a 1-slot block. Each String is 24 bytes, so slot 1 starts at offset 24, exactly the end.
scenes.output: error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: attempting to access 24 bytes, but got alloc40502+0x18 which is at or beyond the end of the allocation of size 24 bytes

scenes.caption: Bug 3: delete line 8. The block is freed, but the 4 live Strings never drop. No UB, so the test passes, and then Miri's leak check fires once per String.
scenes.output:
test tests::push_pop_strings ... ok
error: memory leaked: alloc40726 (Rust heap, size: 1, align: 1)
... (4 in total)
error: aborting due to 4 previous errors

blocks.md: [`MaybeUninit<T>`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html) is std's type for *memory that may not hold a valid T yet*. The compiler assumes every variable of type T holds a valid T: a `&i32` must be non-null and aligned, so `let x: &i32 = mem::zeroed()` is undefined behavior at once, even unused. MyVec never needs it because it only touches empty slots through raw pointers with `write` and `read`. Reach for `MaybeUninit` when uninitialized memory must sit in a typed variable or array, such as `[MaybeUninit<T>; 16]` filled one element at a time.

Two more marker details. **Send and Sync**: `NonNull` is a raw pointer, so MyVec is not Send or Sync automatically. The Rustonomicon's version adds `unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for Vec<T> {}` and the same for Sync, justified because the vector owns its elements uniquely, as a Box would. **PhantomData** (a zero-size field that tells the compiler a type acts as if it held a T): older guides added `PhantomData<T>` so drop checking would know Vec owns Ts. The [Rustonomicon](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/phantom-data.html) now says that since RFC 1238 (an RFC, request for comments, is Rust's formal design proposal) a `Drop` impl already tells the compiler that, so the field is superfluous for drop checking.

Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

MyVec is a teaching subset. It rejects zero-sized types, has no insert, remove, iterators or slice access, and does not handle a panic in the middle of an operation. The Rustonomicon's later Vec chapters add each of these, which is a measure of how much care std's Vec holds.

blocks.question: In `Drop`, what goes wrong if you call `dealloc` first and then pop the remaining elements?
options: Nothing, the order of the two steps does not matter
The elements leak but nothing else happens
Each `pop` reads a String from a block already returned to the allocator: use after free
`dealloc` fails because len is not 0
blocks.explain: After `dealloc` the block belongs to the allocator again. `pop` then calls `ptr::read` on freed memory and drops whatever bytes it finds, which is undefined behavior. Live elements must be dropped while their memory is still valid.

blocks.question: `pop` does `self.len -= 1` and then `ptr::read` on slot `len`. Why is the element not dropped twice, once by the caller and once by `Drop` later?
options: `ptr::read` zeroes the slot after copying
Strings cannot be dropped twice
`Drop` skips slots that hold a moved-out value
After the decrement, len no longer covers that slot, so Drop treats it as empty
blocks.explain: `ptr::read` copies the bits and leaves them in place. What stops a double drop is invariant 2: only the first len slots count as initialized. Decrementing len first moves ownership of that slot's value to the caller.

lessons.title: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership

blocks.md: A **foreign function interface** (FFI) lets code in one language call functions in another. Rust declares C functions in an `unsafe extern "C"` block. The `"C"` names the **ABI** (application binary interface): how arguments travel in registers and on the stack. Every function in that block is unsafe to call (unless you mark it `safe`, a promise the compiler cannot check), because C enforces none of Rust's rules.

blocks.caption: Runs and prints 5, then "handoff". The only unsafe lines are the two calls whose contracts the comments explain.

blocks.md: `CString` is Rust's owned string for C: a heap buffer of bytes ending in a NUL (zero) byte, the terminator C functions such as `strlen` scan for. Two ownership patterns appear here. **Borrowing across the boundary**: `as_ptr()` gives C a pointer while Rust keeps ownership, so the CString must outlive the call. **Transferring across the boundary**: `into_raw()` hands the buffer to C, and only `CString::from_raw` on that same pointer may free it. Rule of thumb from the CString docs: memory goes back to the allocator that produced it, so a buffer allocated by a C library is freed with that library's free function, never with `CString::from_raw`.

blocks.title: Who owns the bytes as a string crosses into C

scenes.caption: `CString::new("hello")` copies the text into a fresh heap buffer and appends a NUL byte (6 bytes). It fails if the text already contains a NUL.
`as_ptr()` lends C a read-only pointer. Rust still owns the buffer; the pointer is only valid while `owned` is alive.
C walks bytes until the NUL and returns 5. Nothing was transferred.
A second CString, "handoff" (8 bytes with its NUL), is made and `into_raw()` consumes it: Rust gives up ownership and will not free the buffer. Forgetting to take it back is a leak.
Wrong: calling C's `free()` on it. The CString docs forbid this; the buffer came from Rust's allocator, which need not be C's malloc.
Right: the pointer returns and `CString::from_raw` retakes ownership exactly once. When `back` is dropped, Rust's allocator frees it.

blocks.question: This compiles with no unsafe on the first line: `let p = CString::new("Hi").unwrap().as_ptr();` then later `unsafe { strlen(p) }`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, `as_ptr` keeps the string alive
`CString::new` must be in an unsafe block
`strlen` needs `*mut c_char`, so it fails to compile
The temporary CString is dropped at the end of the first statement, so `p` dangles and `strlen(p)` is undefined behavior
blocks.explain: A raw pointer carries no lifetime, so the borrow checker cannot connect `p` to the temporary. The docs of `CStr`, the borrowed counterpart of `CString`, use this exact example as a warning. Bind the CString to a variable that lives past the call, as `c_len` does.

blocks.md:
Types that cross the boundary need a layout both sides agree on. Rust's default layout makes almost no promises, so structs shared with C are marked `#[repr(C)]`, which uses C's ordering and padding rules.

The rule, as the Rust Reference states it for `repr(C)`: walk the fields in declaration order; if the current offset is not a multiple of the field's **alignment** (for primitive integers, their size: 1 for u8, 2 for u16, 4 for u32), add padding until it is, place the field, and advance by its size. The struct's alignment is its largest field alignment, and its size is the final offset rounded up to a multiple of that. For `{ u8 flag; u32 id; u16 port; }`: flag at 0, pad to 4, id at 4 to 8, port at 8 to 10, round 10 up to a multiple of 4: **12 bytes**.

blocks.title: struct { u8 flag; u32 id; u16 port; } in memory

scenes.caption: `#[repr(C)]` follows C's rule: fields in declaration order, each at the next multiple of its alignment. flag at 0, id at 4, port at 8; size 12, of which 5 bytes are padding. clang gives the identical layout.
Default Rust layout only promises non-overlapping fields; the order is up to the compiler. rustc 1.90 put id at 0, port at 4, flag at 6: size 8. Never pass such a struct to C.

blocks.md:
Pointers that C may set to NULL map neatly onto `Option`: the std docs guarantee `Option<&T>`, `Option<Box<T>>`, `Option<NonNull<T>>` and `Option<extern "C" fn(..)>` use null for None and have the pointer's ABI, so a nullable callback can be declared without any `transmute` (the unsafe std function that reinterprets one type's bits as another type).

Going the other way, `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn name()` exports a Rust function under a plain symbol name that C can link against. By default rustc *mangles* symbol names, encoding the module path and a hash into them; `no_mangle` turns that off.

Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are one of the most common reasons real code needs unsafe, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

Typical shape of a good binding: a private `extern` block with the raw C signatures, then a public safe wrapper per function that converts types (`&str` to `CString`, null to `None`), checks the C contract, and owns any resource in a struct whose `Drop` calls the C library's free function. The next lesson builds exactly that for a real C library.

blocks.question: A C library returns `char *` from `lib_get_name()` and documents that callers must release it with `lib_free_name()`. How should the Rust wrapper free it?
options: Call `lib_free_name` (for example from a `Drop` impl) after copying the bytes out
Wrap it with `CString::from_raw` and let Rust drop it
Call `libc::free`, since all C strings come from malloc
Leave it: Rust frees foreign memory automatically at scope end
blocks.explain: `CString::from_raw` is only for pointers produced by `CString::into_raw`; on foreign memory it risks allocator corruption. The library may not use malloc at all, so its own release function is the only correct one. Rust never frees memory it does not own.

blocks.question: Using C's layout rules, what is `sizeof` of `struct { uint8_t flag; uint32_t id; uint16_t port; }` on a typical 64-bit target?
options: 7 bytes, the sum of the fields
8 bytes
12 bytes
16 bytes
blocks.explain: flag sits at offset 0, then 3 padding bytes so `id` (alignment 4) starts at 4, `port` follows at 8 and ends at 10, and the total rounds up to the struct alignment 4: 12 bytes. Rust's default layout reordered the same fields into 8 bytes, which is why FFI structs need `#[repr(C)]`.

lessons.title: FFI in a real project: bindgen, build scripts, callbacks and panics

blocks.md: Lesson 7 declared one libc function by hand. A real C library arrives as a header with many functions, `.c` files to compile, **opaque handles** (a struct the header names but never defines, so callers can only hold pointers to it) and callbacks. The tiny example is a **ring buffer**: a fixed-capacity queue stored in an array whose end wraps around to the start.

blocks.caption: csrc/ring.h. The 40-line ring.c behind it mallocs the struct and an int array, and rb_free frees both. `void *user` is C's way to hand the callback some context.

blocks.md: Three tools turn this into a Rust crate. A **build script** is a `build.rs` file at the package root that Cargo compiles and runs before building the package; it talks to Cargo by printing lines that start with `cargo::` and writes generated files to `OUT_DIR`. The **cc** crate compiles C files with the platform's compiler into a **static archive** (a `.a` bundle of object files linked into the final binary). **bindgen** reads a C header through libclang and generates the matching Rust declarations; **libclang** is the clang compiler's C parser packaged as a library. Both go under `[build-dependencies]`.

blocks.caption: build.rs, built and run as shown. bindgen needs libclang installed on the build machine; on macOS the Xcode command line tools provide it.

blocks.title: cargo build for a crate that wraps C

scenes.caption: Before compiling the crate, Cargo builds and runs `build.rs`. Its dependencies (`cc`, `bindgen`) come from `[build-dependencies]`, separate from the crate's own.

The `cc` crate invokes the platform C compiler on ring.c and archives the result as libring.a, then prints the `cargo:` lines (the older one-colon form Cargo still accepts) that tell rustc to link it.
`bindgen` parses ring.h with libclang (the C compiler's parser as a library) and writes Rust `extern` declarations to bindings.rs in `OUT_DIR`, the build script's output folder.
rustc compiles the crate with `include!` pulling in bindings.rs, and the linker combines it with libring.a into one executable. Change ring.c and `rerun-if-changed` makes Cargo rerun the script.

blocks.caption: Real bindgen output, abridged. The opaque struct becomes a zero-size type you can only point at, size_t becomes usize, and the nullable callback becomes Option<extern fn> (lesson 7: None is NULL).

blocks.md: The generated items are all unsafe raw C. The safe layer is hand-written, following lesson 7's shape. `Ring` owns a `NonNull<ffi::ring>`: `new` turns a NULL from `rb_new` into `None`, and `Drop` calls `rb_free` exactly once. The type is not `Clone`, so two owners of one handle, and with them a double free, cannot be written in safe code. Raw pointers are not Send, so `Ring` is not Send either until you check that the C library tolerates use from another thread.

blocks.caption: The wrapper (pop is similar). With cap 3, pushing 10, 20, 30, 40 printed `full, dropped 40`; pop returned Some(10); pushing 50 left 20, 30, 50.

blocks.md: Callbacks are where FFI gets interesting. C can call only a plain function pointer, but a Rust closure is a struct of captured variables plus code. The standard bridge is a **trampoline**: a generic `extern "C" fn trampoline<F>` that C can call, which casts the `void *user` argument back to the closure and calls it. The Rustonomicon's FFI chapter shows the same idea with a pointer to a Rust object. The pointer is valid only as long as the Rust value lives: here C uses it only during `rb_for_each`, so a stack variable is enough. To keep a panic out of C, the trampoline runs the closure inside `std::panic::catch_unwind`, which turns a panic into an `Err` value; `AssertUnwindSafe` is the wrapper that tells the compiler the captured state may be observed after a panic.

blocks.title: A Rust closure called back from C

scenes.caption: The ring holds 20, 30, 50. `for_each` passes C two things: the address of `trampoline::<F>`, a plain `extern "C"` function, and `&mut ctx` cast to `void *`.
C knows nothing about closures. It calls the function pointer with the element and the opaque `user` pointer it was given.
The trampoline casts `user` back to `&mut Ctx<F>` (sound only because it really is one, alive for the whole call) and calls the closure.
The same round trip for 30 and 50. The closure's captured `sum` reaches 100.
C returns. Rust's `ctx` is still on the stack, so the pointer C held was valid throughout, and C kept no copy of it.
If the closure panics, the trampoline's `catch_unwind` stops the panic before it reaches C's frame and stores it in ctx; `for_each` re-raises it with `resume_unwind` after C has returned.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the trampoline simply calls the closure, with no `catch_unwind`, and the closure panics on the value 50. The panic tries to unwind out of the `extern "C"` trampoline toward `rb_for_each`, a C frame. What happens?
blocks.reveal:
The process **aborts**. Our run printed the panic message `bad value 50`, then `panic in a function that cannot unwind` and `thread caused non-unwinding panic. aborting.`, and exited with status 134 (SIGABRT). `Ring`'s Drop never ran.

The Rustonomicon states the rule: when a Rust panic reaches an ABI boundary that is not allowed to unwind, such as `extern "C"`, the process aborts safely. A foreign exception (from C++) crossing into Rust that way is undefined behavior.

blocks.caption: Panic-safe version (imports of `Any`, `c_int`, `c_void`, `catch_unwind`, `resume_unwind` and `AssertUnwindSafe` omitted). `r.for_each(|v| sum += v)` gave sum 100; the panicking closure now ends in an ordinary panic (exit status 101) that runs Ring's Drop on the way out.

blocks.md: The other choice is `extern "C-unwind"`, which declares that unwinding may cross the boundary. Use it only when the other side is built to be unwound through, such as C++ code that should run its destructors; for plain C, catch the panic. Note that a crate built with `panic=abort` aborts at the panic itself, whatever the ABI.

Strings that C owns come back as `const char *`. [`CStr::from_ptr`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.CStr.html) wraps one without copying or taking ownership: the borrowed counterpart of lesson 7's `CString`. Its contract: a NUL terminator inside one allocation, a non-null pointer, and no mutation while borrowed. The returned lifetime is inferred, so the docs advise tying it to the owner. Copy out with `to_str()` or `to_owned()`, then free the original with the library's own function.

The reverse direction, C calling Rust, uses `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn` in a crate built as `crate-type = ["staticlib"]`. **cbindgen**, from Mozilla, generates the C header from the Rust source, so the two cannot drift apart.

blocks.caption: Ran with cbindgen 0.29.4: 532 is the sum of the bytes of hello. cbindgen also copies the doc comment into the header.

blocks.md: Checklist for wrapping a C library: build.rs with cc and bindgen; a private ffi module; one owning struct per handle with Drop calling the library's free; NULL mapped to None and error codes to Result; callbacks through a trampoline that catches panics; Send and Sync added only after reading the library's threading rules.

blocks.question: A C library's `rb_set_listener(rb, cb, user)` stores the callback and `user` pointer and calls them later, on every push. Your wrapper passes `&mut closure` from a local variable, as `for_each` does. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the closure is captured by value inside the trampoline
When the wrapper function returns, the closure is gone but C still holds `user`; the next push calls through a dangling pointer
It fails to compile because `&mut` cannot be cast to `*mut c_void`
C copies the closure into its own memory, so it is merely leaked
blocks.explain: A raw pointer carries no lifetime, so the compiler cannot connect `user` to the local. For a stored callback, put the closure on the heap (`Box::into_raw`), keep it alive while registered, and free it with `Box::from_raw` when unregistering or in Drop.

blocks.question: In which step does bindgen run, and what does it need?
options: At build time, inside build.rs, and it needs libclang on the build machine
At run time, the first time an extern function is called
Inside rustc itself, with no extra dependency
Only once by hand; its output must be committed and it cannot run in build.rs
blocks.explain: The bindgen guide describes it as a library that leverages libclang to parse C headers; called from build.rs it regenerates bindings on each relevant build. Committing pre-generated bindings is a valid alternative that avoids the libclang dependency, but it is not required.
